item.title: Kibidango: Momotaro's Millet Dumplings — Guide
item.description: Kibidango are small, soft, faintly sweet mochi dumplings dusted in powder, and in Okayama they carry a story: in the tale of Momotaro, the Peach Boy, it is kibidango that the hero gives to a dog, a monkey and a pheasant to win them as companions on his journey to defeat the demons. Since the Kibi Plain west of Okayama is widely held to be the origin of that legend, the dumplings have become the prefecture’s defining souvenir.

item.title: Momiji Manju: Miyajima's Maple-Leaf Cakes — Guide
item.description: Momiji manju are little cakes baked in the shape of a maple leaf, a nod to the maples of Momijidani, and they are the definitive souvenir of Hiroshima. Created on Miyajima over a century ago, they are made from a light castella-style sponge batter poured into leaf-shaped moulds and filled traditionally with sweet red bean paste, though modern fillings run to custard, chocolate, matcha and cheese. On Miyajima you can watch them being made on rotating griddles and eat them still warm, which is a completely different experience from the boxed ones — and several shops sell them battered and deep-fried on a stick as age-momiji.

item.title: Narazuke: Nara's Amber Sake-Lees Pickles — Guide
item.description: Narazuke are Nara’s celebrated sake-lees pickles, one of the city’s oldest food traditions, dating back over a thousand years to when temple brewers preserved vegetables in the fragrant lees (kasu) left over from making sake. Melon, cucumber, ginger, gourd and other vegetables are repeatedly re-pickled in fresh sake lees over months or even years, slowly turning a deep translucent amber and taking on a complex, richly aromatic flavour — sweet, savoury, and distinctly boozy.

item.title: Miyagi Tansu: Iron-Fitted Traditional Cabinetry — Guide
item.description: Miyagi tansu are traditional wooden chests renowned across Japan for their lustrous zelkova (keyaki) wood grain and elaborate hand-forged iron fittings, crafted using techniques passed down since the Edo period. Each piece can take months to complete, with the wood aged and polished to a deep reddish sheen and the iron hardware hand-hammered into intricate patterns — a genuine heirloom-quality craft still practised by a small number of Sendai-area workshops.

item.title: Iburigakko: Akita's Smoked Daikon Pickles — Guide
item.description: Iburigakko is a beloved Akita farmhouse specialty — daikon radish smoke-dried over wood fires, then pickled in rice bran, producing a crunchy, deeply smoky, gently sweet pickle. Traditionally made in snowbound winter farmhouses where radishes couldn’t sun-dry, it pairs superbly with sake and, in a modern twist, with cream cheese. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Inland Akita (Yokote etc.) Hours Shop hours Admission Cheap (packs) Time needed About 20 min Best time Year-round; made in winter What to Try Crunchy, smoky pickled daikon slices.

item.title: Nanbu Senbei: Iwate's Iron-Molded Wheat Crackers — Guide
item.description: Nanbu senbei are crisp, round wheat crackers baked in iron molds, a rustic staple of the historic Nanbu region spanning northern Iwate and Aomori. Often studded with sesame or peanuts, they come plain, sweet, or savory, and the puffed rim (mimi) is a favourite. A cheap, tasty and very portable Iwate souvenir. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Northern Iwate & Morioka Hours Shop hours Admission Cheap (packs of crackers) Time needed About 20 min Best time Year-round What to Try Crisp round wheat crackers with sesame or peanut.
